It details a 'Method' section including Participants, Material, Procedure, and Analysis (p. 57).
It presents 'Results' from 'Dissimilarity Analysis', 'Linguistic Analysis', and 'Acoustic Analysis' (p. 58-59).
It includes figures like 'Additive tree representation' and 'Two-dimensional MDS representation' of experimental data (p. 58, 59).

title: Categorization of Environmental Sounds

findings.antecedent: Complex urban environmental sounds (mixture of traffic and human sounds)
findings.consequent: Categorization into two main groups: 'human activity' dominated soundscapes and 'traffic noise' dominated soundscapes
findings.source: abstract, Results - Dissimilarity Analysis, Results - Linguistic Analysis, Discussion
findings.quote: Two main categories emerged from the free-sort, reflecting the absence or presence of human activity in relation to hedonic judgments.

findings.antecedent: Dominance of human activity sounds in soundscapes
findings.quote: the human activity category was spontaneously described as pleasant (8 occurrences)

findings.antecedent: Dominance of traffic noise in soundscapes
findings.quote: the traffic noise category was described as unpleasant (17 occurrences).

findings.consequent: Subcategorization into script categories based on social activities performed (e.g., 'do groceries', 'have a drink', 'take a walk') and location types (e.g., 'market', 'café', 'park'), reflecting a dimension of tranquillity
findings.quote: human activity samples were subcategorized into script categories by 75% of the participants on the basis of the type of activities performed

findings.consequent: Subcategorization based on the presence/absence of human sounds (linked to pleasantness) or type of vehicles
findings.quote: Half of the participants subcategorized traffic samples on the basis of the presence of human sounds in relation to the judgments of pleasantness

findings.consequent: Categorization primarily based on high-level semantic features (source identification, meaning, context) rather than low-level psychoacoustic parameters (e.g., loudness, spectral centroid)
findings.quote: No significant interaction between psychoacoustic parameters and category membership was observed. ... semantic features overpowered perceptual attributes, and no effect of loudness was observed.

findings.antecedent: Lack of simple lexicalized terms for auditory phenomena in French
findings.consequent: Participants use complex phrasings constructed on source denominations in verbal descriptions
findings.quote: Given the lack of simple lexicalized linguistic forms available in French to describe auditory phenomena... participants make use of complex phrasings

findings.antecedent: Multichannel surround sound reproduction providing a strong feeling of immersion
findings.consequent: Urban noise reproduced in a laboratory setting is processed as in everyday life situations (ecological validity)
findings.quote: Guastavino et al. (2005) further showed that a multichannel surround sound reproduction, providing a strong feeling of immersion, was necessary to ensure that urban noise reproduced in a laboratory setting be processed as in everyday life situations.

limitations: Categorical structure was not tested in a strict sense with stimuli ranging along a physical continuum due to the complex structure of urban soundscapes where noise stems simultaneously from a variety of sources (p. 60).

Further research is required to investigate the complex relationship between linguistic and cognitive categories, specifically how individual sensory experiences are objectivized in language when elaborating shared cognitive categories (p. 61).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated how people categorize complex urban environmental sounds using a free categorization task with open-ended verbal descriptions. Findings revealed two main categories: soundscapes dominated by human activity and those dominated by traffic noise, with distinct hedonic judgments (pleasant for human activity, unpleasant for traffic). Subcategories were mediated by social activities and locations for human activity sounds, and by human sound presence/absence or vehicle type for traffic sounds. Categorization was primarily driven by high-level semantic features (source identification, meaning, context) rather than low-level psychoacoustic parameters. The study highlights the role of cognitive factors, situational context, and linguistic constraints in auditory categorization. Limitations include the inability to test categorical structure along a physical continuum due to the complex nature of urban soundscapes.
